children: Eurozone industrial output fell again in July, highlighting the uneven nature of the region's economic recovery as manufacturers contend with higher energy costs despite signs of improving demand.

Industrial production fell 0.1% from the previous month, following a 0.1% decline in June, the statistics agency Eurostat said Wednesday. A consensus of economists polled by The Wall Street Journal expected a steeper fall of 0.4%.

The decline came despite signs that some manufacturers are becoming more optimistic about the outlook. According to purchasing managers' surveys by S&P Global, activity in the eurozone's manufacturing sector picked up in July and expanded at its fastest pace in more than four years in August.

The divergence between the survey data and official production figures partly reflects the weakness of some of Europe's biggest industrial economies. Production in Germany--the eurozone's largest economy--fell 1.5% on month in July, while output also retreated 0.4% in France, Eurostat data showed.

"The latest industrial production figures are hardly disastrous, but they do underline a picture of lost momentum," said Bert Colijn, an economist at ING, in a note. Weakness in consumer-oriented industries was particularly striking, he added.

Manufacturers have faced unusually difficult conditions over the summer. Extreme heat pushed water levels on Germany's Rhine river to record lows, disrupting an important transport route for industrial goods and adding to logistics costs. German producer prices also rose sharply in July as the impact of the war in the Middle East continued to feed through to industry.

According to Capital Economics economist Megan Fisher, the decline in July was due to a significant fall in auto production due to the temporary shutdown of a plant in Germany, which is expected to rebound in August.

Still, some European producers have continued to benefit from companies bringing forward orders to get ahead of potentially higher prices and supply shortages. Economists say greater disruptions to Asian competitors from the Iran conflict have also supported demand for some European manufacturers.

Eurozone production is also being supported by large-scale industrial investment in Germany, as the government seeks to rebuild the country's manufacturing base while rapidly expanding military spending in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The 21-nation currency area's economy has held up better than expected since the outbreak of the war in the Middle East. Gross domestic product rose 0.6% in the second quarter, boosted by a 3.4% jump in exports compared with the first quarter. On an annualized basis, the economy expanded around 2.6%, outpacing the U.S.

But higher energy costs continue to present hurdles for industry. Eurozone inflation accelerated to 3.3% in August--its highest level in almost three years. The price of Brent crude oil moved back above $100 in recent days, adding upward pressure to production costs.
Domestic producer prices for energy rose by 5.6% on month in July, with prices likely to have risen further since then, Capital Economics' Fisher said.

The European Central Bank has now raised interest rates twice since the war began, placing an additional burden on industrial activity. At its most recent meeting last week, the central bank said it expects the energy shock to push inflation to a peak of 3.6% in the fourth quarter, and revised up its forecasts for 2027 and 2028.
